section.title: The Trial, Crucifixion, and Burial
section.sectionRationale: The Gospel reaches its goal. Jesus is handed to Pilate, condemned in place of Barabbas, mocked as a king, and crucified at Golgotha. Darkness falls, and He cries out the anguish of forsakenness before He dies. At His death the temple veil is torn from top to bottom, and a Gentile centurion confesses Him the Son of God, the confession Mark has been driving toward from his first verse. Joseph of Arimathea lays Him in a tomb.
section.thesis: The King of the Jews reigns from a cross: condemned though innocent, dying in the place of a guilty man, forsaken by God so that His people need not be, and at His death the barrier to God is torn open and a Gentile soldier confesses Him the Son of God.
section.frameNote: Six beats: the trial before Pilate; the crowd's choice of Barabbas; the mocking by the soldiers; the crucifixion and mockery at the cross; the death of Jesus, the torn veil, and the centurion's confession; and the burial by Joseph of Arimathea.

units.label: The trial before Pilate
units.note: are You the King of the Jews

verses.text: Early in the morning, the chief priests, elders, scribes, and the whole Sanhedrin devised a plan. They bound Jesus, led Him away, and handed Him over to Pilate.
So Pilate questioned Him, “Are You the King of the Jews?” “You have said so,” Jesus replied.
And the chief priests began to accuse Him of many things.
Then Pilate questioned Him again, “Have You no answer? Look how many charges they are bringing against You!”
But to Pilate’s amazement, Jesus made no further reply.
Now it was Pilate’s custom at the feast to release to the people a prisoner of their choosing.
And a man named {{barabbas|Barabbas}} was imprisoned with the rebels who had committed murder during the insurrection.
So the crowd went up and began asking Pilate to keep his custom.
“Do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?” Pilate asked.
For he knew it was out of envy that the chief priests had handed Jesus over.
But the chief priests stirred up the crowd to have him release Barabbas to them instead.
So Pilate asked them again, “What then do you want me to do with the One you call the King of the Jews?”
And they shouted back, “Crucify Him!”
“Why?” asked Pilate. “What evil has He done?” But they shouted all the louder, “Crucify Him!”
And wishing to satisfy the crowd, Pilate released Barabbas to them. But he had Jesus flogged, and handed Him over to be crucified.
Then the soldiers led Jesus away into the palace (that is, the Praetorium) and called the whole company together.
They dressed Him in a purple robe, twisted together a crown of thorns, and set it on His head.
And they began to salute Him: “Hail, King of the Jews!”
They kept striking His head with a staff and spitting on Him. And they knelt down and bowed before Him.
After they had mocked Him, they removed the purple robe and put His own clothes back on Him. Then they led Him out to crucify Him.

units.label: The crucifixion and the mockery
units.note: He saved others, but He cannot save Himself

verses.text: Now Simon of Cyrene, the father of Alexander and Rufus, was passing by on his way in from the country, and the soldiers forced him to carry the cross of Jesus.
They brought Jesus to a place called {{golgotha|Golgotha}}, which means The Place of the Skull.
There they offered Him wine mixed with myrrh, but He did not take it.
And they {{stauroo|crucified}} Him. They also divided His garments by casting lots to decide what each of them would take.
It was the third hour when they crucified Him.
And the charge inscribed against Him read: THE KING OF THE JEWS.
Along with Jesus, they crucified two robbers, one on His right and one on His left.
And those who passed by heaped abuse on Him, shaking their heads and saying, “Aha! You who are going to destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days,
come down from the cross and save Yourself!”
In the same way, the chief priests and scribes mocked Him among themselves, saying, “He saved others, but He cannot save Himself!
Let the Christ, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross, so that we may see and believe!” And even those who were crucified with Him berated Him.

units.label: The death of Jesus and the torn veil
units.note: truly this man was the Son of God

verses.text: From the sixth hour until the ninth hour darkness came over all the land.
At the ninth hour, Jesus cried out in a loud voice, “{{eloi|Eloi}}, Eloi, lema sabachthani?” which means, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”
When some of those standing nearby heard this, they said, “Behold, He is calling Elijah.”
And someone ran and filled a sponge with sour wine. He put it on a reed and held it up for Jesus to drink, saying, “Leave Him alone. Let us see if Elijah comes to take Him down.”
But Jesus let out a loud cry and breathed His last.
And the {{katapetasma|veil}} of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom.
When the centurion standing there in front of Jesus saw how He had breathed His last, he said, “Truly this man was the Son of God!”
And there were also women watching from a distance. Among them were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome.
These women had followed Jesus and ministered to Him while He was in Galilee, and there were many other women who had come up to Jerusalem with Him.

units.label: The burial by Joseph of Arimathea
units.note: laid in a tomb cut from the rock

verses.text: Now it was already evening. Since it was Preparation Day (that is, the day before the Sabbath),
Joseph of Arimathea, a prominent Council member who himself was waiting for the kingdom of God, boldly went to Pilate to ask for the body of Jesus.
Pilate was surprised to hear that Jesus was already dead, so he summoned the centurion to ask if this was so.
When Pilate had confirmed it with the centurion, he granted the body to Joseph.

So Joseph bought a linen cloth, took down the body of Jesus, wrapped it in the cloth, and placed it in a tomb that had been cut out of the rock. Then he rolled a stone against the entrance to the tomb.
Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joseph saw where His body was placed.

barabbas.gloss: Barabbas, meaning son of the father, a murderer and insurrectionist. In a striking exchange the guilty son of the father goes free while the true Son of the Father dies in his place, a living picture of substitution: the innocent condemned so the guilty may be released.

golgotha.gloss: Golgotha, the Place of the Skull, the site outside Jerusalem where Jesus was crucified. Mark preserves the Aramaic name and translates it, grounding the event in a real place and time; here the King of the Jews is enthroned on a cross.

stauroo.gloss: To crucify, to execute on a cross. Crucifixion was Rome's most shameful and agonizing punishment, reserved for slaves and rebels. That the Son of God dies this death shows the depth of His humiliation and the seriousness of the sin He bears in His people's place.

eloi.gloss: My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me, the opening of Psalm 22 cried in Aramaic. Jesus voices the anguish of bearing God's judgment, truly forsaken so that His people never will be, yet praying a psalm that ends in vindication and worldwide worship.

katapetasma.gloss: The veil or curtain of the temple that barred the way into the Most Holy Place, God's symbolic dwelling. Torn from top to bottom at Jesus' death, by God's own hand, it signals that the way to God is now open through the death of His Son, and that the old temple order is ending.

basic.context: The leaders hand Jesus to Pilate, who asks if He is the King of the Jews. Jesus barely answers, and Pilate marvels. Following a feast custom, Pilate offers to release a prisoner; the crowd, stirred up by the priests, chooses the murderer Barabbas and demands that Jesus be crucified. Pilate, wanting to please the crowd, has Jesus flogged and handed over. Soldiers mock Him as a king with a purple robe and crown of thorns. At Golgotha they crucify Him between two robbers, cast lots for His clothes, and mock Him to save Himself. Darkness covers the land, and Jesus cries out, My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me, then dies. The temple veil tears in two, and a Gentile centurion says, Truly this man was the Son of God. Joseph of Arimathea buries Him in a rock tomb as the women watch.
basic.hermeneutics: This is the climax of Mark's Gospel and the answer to its opening line: this crucified man is the Son of God. Irony runs throughout: Jesus is mocked as King precisely when He is reigning from the cross, and told to save Himself when His refusal to do so is how He saves others. Barabbas dramatizes substitution. The torn veil and the centurion's confession interpret the death: access to God is opened, and the truth is confessed by a Gentile.
basic.originalLanguages: Barabbas, son of the father, goes free while the true Son dies. Jesus is stauroo, crucified, at golgotha, the Place of the Skull. He cries eloi, my God, in the words of Psalm 22, and at His death the katapetasma, the temple veil, is torn.
basic.typology: The innocent dying for the guilty fulfils the substitution pictured in the Passover and Isaiah 53. The dividing of garments and the cry of dereliction fulfil Psalm 22. The torn veil fulfils and ends the temple's separation, opening access to God.
basic.christ: Jesus is the King enthroned on a cross, the innocent substitute for the guilty, the forsaken Son who bears God's judgment, and the Son of God confessed at last. He saves others by refusing to save Himself.
basic.god: God works His salvation through the cross, tearing the veil by His own hand to open the way to Himself. God forsakes His Son in judgment so that sinners may be welcomed.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 22 supplies the cry and the divided garments. Isaiah 53 foretells the substitute numbered with transgressors. Hebrews 10 interprets the torn veil.
basic.oneStory: Everything the Gospel has built toward arrives here: the Son of God dies as King, in the place of the guilty, forsaken so His people need not be. The veil that kept sinners from God is torn open, and a Gentile confesses the truth Mark announced in his first verse. The story now waits, with the women, at a sealed tomb, for the third day.

context.literary:
Mark 15 is built on the clock. Before dawn the Sanhedrin consults and binds Jesus, verse 1; the third hour, about nine in the morning, is when they crucify Him, verse 25; the sixth hour brings the darkness, verse 33; the ninth hour brings the cry and the death, verses 34 to 37; and evening falls on Preparation Day, verse 42. After the slow, scene by scene pace of earlier chapters, Mark now counts hours like a man at a bedside, and the reader is held in the long afternoon.

Two scenes of rejection frame the cross. Before it come Pilate, the crowd and the soldiers; after it come the passers by, the priests and the two robbers, verses 29 to 32. The mockery is thrice repeated, and each group reaches for a title: King of the Jews from the soldiers, Christ and King of Israel from the priests. Every taunt is true, and every taunt is aimed at the wrong target. That is Mark's irony at full stretch.

The chapter is also a mirror of the baptism. At the start of the Gospel the heavens were torn open and a voice from heaven said, 'You are My beloved Son,' Mark 1:10-11. Here the temple veil is torn and a human voice says, 'Truly this man was the Son of God!' verses 38 and 39. The same Greek verb for tearing is used in both places. Between those two tearings lies the whole Gospel.

Notice who is missing. The Twelve have vanished since Gethsemane. Their place is taken by a Cyrenian conscripted from the roadside, verse 21, a Gentile soldier, verse 39, a council member who had been waiting, verse 43, and women watching from a distance, verse 40. The chapter ends with Jesus in a tomb and the women looking at it, verse 47, and nothing in the narrative yet says what comes next.
context.historical:
Pilate governed Judea as prefect from about AD 26 to 36, answerable to Rome and often in tension with the people he ruled. He normally lived on the coast and came up to Jerusalem at the great feasts, when crowds and revolutionary hopes ran high. That is why the Sanhedrin brings its case to him at Passover. A Jewish court could pronounce on blasphemy, but the charge laid before Rome has to be political, which is why the title King of the Jews is pressed in verse 2 and ends up on the cross in verse 26.

Crucifixion was a Roman penalty, reserved for slaves, rebels and those without citizenship, and designed to shame as well as kill. Flogging with a lead tipped whip usually came first, and victims commonly carried the crossbeam to the place of execution, which is why soldiers needed to commandeer help when Jesus could not, verse 21. Simon came from Cyrene, in North Africa, and Mark names his sons Alexander and Rufus as if his first readers knew them. A Rufus is greeted in the church at Rome in Romans 16:13, which may be the same family, though the text does not say so.

The 'custom' of releasing a prisoner at the feast, verse 6, is known to us only from the Gospels, so we cannot check it elsewhere. It fits what we know of Roman governors, who sometimes bought calm with gestures of clemency. Barabbas had been among rebels who 'committed murder during the insurrection,' verse 7, so the crowd choosing him is choosing the revolutionary option over the man who refused a sword.

A body hung on a tree was not to stay there overnight, Deuteronomy 21:22-23, and the Sabbath was about to begin at sundown. This is why Joseph of Arimathea moves in haste, verses 42 to 46. Crucified bodies were normally left to the elements or thrown into common graves, so burial in a rock cut tomb was an honour, and Pilate's surprise that death had come so soon, verse 44, shows how unusual the speed was.
context.canonical:
Mark 15 is the most densely scriptural stretch of the Gospel, even though Mark names few citations. The soldiers dividing His clothes by lot, verse 24, and the passers by who shake their heads and taunt Him to let God rescue Him, verses 29 to 32, are drawn from Psalm 22:7-8 and 22:18, and the cry of verse 34 is its opening line. The sour wine, verse 36, recalls Psalm 69:21. The darkness at noon echoes Amos 8:9, where God says He will 'make the sun go down at noon' on the day He judges. Isaiah 53 lies underneath the whole scene: the silent servant, Isaiah 53:7, and the one 'numbered with the transgressors,' Isaiah 53:12, which is the thought verse 28 expresses in manuscripts that include it.

Within Mark the chapter pays off what Jesus has been saying since Caesarea Philippi: the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected, and be killed, Mark 8:31, and has come 'to give His life as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45. The charge about the temple in Mark 14:58 comes back as the taunt of 15:29, and the Son of Man 'sitting at the right hand of Power,' Mark 14:62, is still to be seen.

The rest of the New Testament reads the death through the torn veil and the curse. Paul says Christ 'became a curse for us,' Galatians 3:13, and that God 'made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf,' 2 Corinthians 5:21. Hebrews says the way into the Most Holy Place has been opened 'through the curtain of His body,' Hebrews 10:19-20, and that Jesus suffered outside the city gate, Hebrews 13:12. Peter's sermon in Acts 2:23 and Paul's creed in 1 Corinthians 15:3-4, which includes the burial, both rest on this event.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Mark wrote for believers who were themselves facing the cross in some form, probably in Rome under pressure, and he wanted them to see that the Messiah they followed had gone before them into shame. The chapter answers the objection every hearer would feel: how can a man executed by Rome be the Son of God? Mark's answer is not to soften the cross but to put it at the centre. Everything the soldiers and priests meant as mockery, he lets stand as the truth.

He also meant to correct a false picture of power. Pilate has legions, the priests have the council, the crowd has the voice; Jesus has silence. Yet it is Jesus who is the sovereign figure in the scene, because He goes to the cross knowing what He does, and it is the sentencing powers who are being sentenced by the very verdict they hand down.

Finally, Mark wanted his readers to hear the centurion's words as an invitation. The first complete confession of Jesus as the Son of God in Mark's narrative comes from a Gentile who watched Him die, not from a disciple. A reader sitting in a Roman house church is meant to understand that the way into that confession runs through the cross, and that it is open to people like the centurion and like them.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes events; it issues no commands. The trial, the flogging, the mockery and the crucifixion are what sinful men did, and Mark never presents them as a model. Pilate's weak calculation to 'satisfy the crowd,' verse 15, is a warning, not an example, and the soldiers' cruelty is recorded so that we see what Jesus bore.

What does apply is the shape of the story. Jesus' silence, His refusal to come down, and His refusal of the numbing wine are patterns, in the sense of the call to take up a cross in Mark 8:34, but they are not a rule that every believer must stay mute before authorities. Paul defends himself before governors in Acts. The cross is first of all what Christ did for us, and only then a pattern for us. Nor does the chapter license blaming the Jewish people as a whole, which has been a terrible misuse. The accusers are named as a group of leaders, the crowd is stirred up by them, and the instrument of death is Roman. Mark's own main point is that all hands, Jewish and Gentile, were part of it, and that the same death was for all.

debates.question: What did Jesus mean by the cry 'My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?'

views.label: Real abandonment as He bore judgment
views.case: The words are the first line of Psalm 22:1, but Mark gives them in Aramaic and then translates them, so that no reader can miss them. They come at the end of three hours of darkness, a sign of judgment, as in Amos 8:9. Paul says God made Christ 'to be sin on our behalf,' 2 Corinthians 5:21, and that He became a curse, Galatians 3:13. The Reformers, especially Calvin, held that Jesus truly bore the wrath due to sinners and experienced the loss of the Father's face, without ceasing to be the Son.

views.label: A prayer that quotes the whole psalm
views.case: Quoting the first line of a psalm often brought the whole psalm to mind. Psalm 22 moves from groaning to praise, and ends with all the ends of the earth turning to the LORD, Psalm 22:27, and with His righteousness proclaimed to a people yet unborn, Psalm 22:31. On this reading Jesus is praying in faith, not despair, and His cry already carries the hope of vindication.

views.label: Both together
views.case: Others hold that the cry is a real lament and a real trust at once, as the psalm itself is. The psalmist feels abandoned and still says 'My God' twice. The words 'why' and 'My' sit together, and the verse 'He has not hidden His face from him,' Psalm 22:24, comes only after the experience of hiddenness.

debates.bearing: All three agree that the cry is Scripture on Jesus' lips and that it belongs to the center of the atonement. The strongest reading holds the first and third together: He truly bore the desolation sin deserves, and He did so as the Son who trusted the Father who would raise Him, Mark 9:31.

debates.question: Which veil was torn, and what did the tearing mean?

views.label: The inner veil, opening the Most Holy Place
views.case: The word Mark uses can be read of either curtain, but the language of Hebrews points inward: Jesus 'went through' the tabernacle into the Most Holy Place, Hebrews 9:11-12, and believers enter 'through the curtain of His body,' Hebrews 10:19-20. The tearing means the barrier of Exodus 26:33 has been removed.

views.label: The outer veil, a sign of judgment on the temple
views.case: Some point out that the outer curtain was visible to people in the courts, and that the tearing foreshadows the destruction of the temple that Jesus had foretold, Mark 13:2. On this view the act is a sign of divine judgment, the rending of garments in mourning for the sanctuary's end.

views.label: Both openings and ending
views.case: A third view holds that the sign can carry both meanings, access for all peoples and the close of the old temple system. It is notable that the sign is passive: the veil 'was torn,' by God, not by any human hand.

debates.bearing: Mark does not explain the sign, so we must read it with the rest of Scripture. Whichever veil is meant, the tearing from top to bottom puts the action in God's hands, and the following confession by a Gentile suggests that access is now for the nations, as Mark 11:17 had said.

study.originalLanguages:
Mark leans on one verb through the whole passion, paradidomi, 'hand over.' It is the verb of verse 1, where the leaders hand Jesus to Pilate, of verse 10, where Pilate knows it was out of envy they handed Him over, and of verse 15, where Pilate hands Him over to be crucified. The same verb described what would happen in Mark 9:31 ('delivered into the hands of men'), what Judas did in Mark 14:10, and in Isaiah 53:12 in the Greek Old Testament it describes the servant's soul being given up to death. By the end, every party has handed Jesus to the next, and behind them all is the Father who 'gave Him up for us all,' Romans 8:32. The verb carries both human betrayal and divine purpose, and Mark never separates them.

Mark's vocabulary here is full of Latin, a clue to his Roman readers. The 'palace' is the praitorion, taken from praetorium, verse 16. The verb for flogging, phragelloo, verse 15, comes from the Latin flagellum, the whip. And the centurion is a kenturion, verse 39, another Latin loanword. These Latin words are small signs that Mark wrote to be heard in the capital of the empire that crucified Jesus.

The robbers on either side, verse 27, are lestai. The word is not merely thieves; it describes bandits and violent insurgents. Jesus used it in Mark 11:17 of those who had made the temple 'a den of robbers,' and in Mark 14:48 asked the arresting crowd whether they had come out against Him as against a lestes, an outlaw. He is now executed in company with the lestai, which shows how the authorities have classified Him. Barabbas is among the 'rebels,' verse 7.

The verb for 'torn,' schizo, in verse 38 is the same verb used in Mark 1:10, where the heavens are 'breaking open' at the baptism. The BSB translates the two differently, but Mark writes the same verb and the same divine passive, 'was torn.' These two tearings give the Gospel its frame. The tearing at the beginning is followed by the Father's voice; the tearing at the end is followed by a Gentile's voice.

In verse 34 the cry's last verb, 'forsaken,' is enkataleipo, the verb of the Greek version of Psalm 22:1. It means to leave behind, to desert someone in the place of danger. It is a heavy word, used of leaving a person with no help. Jesus did not choose a softer word from the psalm.

Finally, the centurion's confession, 'Truly this man was the Son of God,' is huios theou without an article in Greek. It can be translated 'a son of God' or 'the Son of God,' and scholars have argued over it for generations. Mark's own use of the phrase, and the fact that the confession comes in response to the manner of Jesus' death, houtos, make the fuller sense the most natural one for the reader, even if the centurion's own grasp was partial.

typology.fulfillment: David's psalm of the abandoned and mocked servant of God contains the very pictures Mark gives us: the shaking heads, Psalm 22:7, the taunt that He should be rescued, 22:8, the divided garments and lots cast for clothing, 22:18. David wrote of his own distress, but the psalm outruns him; no man of his experience had hands and feet pierced, 22:16. In Jesus these details are not decoration but the pattern of the afflicted one completed in a single death. The psalm ends in the praise of the nations, 22:27, which Mark echoes in the centurion. The type falls short in that David was rescued from death, while Jesus passes through it.

The servant is silent before His accusers, Isaiah 53:7, is numbered with the transgressors, 53:12, and is buried with a rich man in His death, 53:9. Mark gives each in turn: Jesus makes no further reply to Pilate, verse 5, is crucified between two robbers, verse 27, and buried by a wealthy council member, verses 43 to 46. Isaiah says the LORD laid on Him 'the iniquity of us all,' 53:6, and that He would 'justify many,' 53:11. The escalation in Jesus is that the servant is not only a model of patient suffering but the sin bearer, Mark 10:45. The type falls short because no prophet or Israel as a nation completed the work; only the Son did.

typology.type: The veil and the tabernacle's separation
typology.fulfillment: The curtain of Exodus 26:31-33, woven with cherubim, 'will separate the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place.' Only the high priest passed it, once a year and never without blood, Hebrews 9:7. Hebrews says that arrangement showed the way into the holiest 'had not yet been disclosed,' 9:8. At the death of Jesus the veil is torn from top to bottom, and the writer says believers enter 'by the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body,' 10:19-20. The type falls short by design: the curtain could only keep sinners out, while Christ's body opens the way in.

typology.type: Isaac spared and the Son not spared
typology.fulfillment: On Mount Moriah Abraham was told to give up his beloved son, and a ram was provided in his place, Genesis 22:12-13. Barabbas is the one who goes free, and Jesus is the one who does not. Paul draws the climax of the Isaac story into the cross: God 'did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all,' Romans 8:32. The correspondence is not exact, since Isaac was reprieved while Jesus died, and Barabbas, unlike Isaac, is a guilty man. That is the escalation: the substitute does not simply stand in for an innocent child but for the guilty, and the Father does not stay Abraham's hand a second time.

study.christ:
The chapter shows Christ as King in the very act of being denied His crown. Pilate's question in verse 2 is the first time anyone in the Gospel has asked Jesus directly whether He is a king, and the answer, 'You have said so,' neither denies nor adopts the political meaning Pilate has in mind. Mark then lets the title run five times through the chapter, in Pilate's mouth, the soldiers' salute, and the sign above the cross, verse 26. The crown is thorns, the robe is purple, the throne is a cross, and the court that attends Him are two robbers, one on the right and one on the left. James and John had once asked for those seats in His glory, Mark 10:37, and Jesus had said it was not His to give, 10:40. Now we see for whom they were prepared.

He is the one who refuses to save Himself in order to save others. The taunt of the priests, 'He saved others, but He cannot save Himself,' verse 31, is unwittingly an exact statement of the gospel. Jesus had taught that 'whoever wants to save his life will lose it,' Mark 8:35, and had said the Son of Man came 'to give His life as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45. He could have come down; He stayed because the ransom could not be paid any other way.

He is the substitute, and Barabbas stands for everyone who is released because someone else is held. Barabbas is a convicted insurrectionist who walks out as Jesus is led in. Mark does not draw the moral out in words. He does not need to. Paul does: 'God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God,' 2 Corinthians 5:21.

He is the Son who is forsaken. In the cry of verse 34 He says 'My God' where in Gethsemane He had said 'Abba, Father,' Mark 14:36. This is the cost of bearing a curse, Galatians 3:13, and Mark does not try to make it gentler.

He is the Son of God confessed. The first human confession of His divine sonship in the narrative comes from a Gentile who saw how He died. It comes from the cross, not from the empty tomb, which has not yet been found. The voice of the Father in Mark 1:11 and 9:7 had declared Jesus Son already; the centurion now says it aloud on earth, and Mark's opening line, 'the Son of God,' Mark 1:1, has its first human echo.

He is buried. Joseph of Arimathea, who had been 'waiting for the kingdom of God,' verse 43, takes the body of the King and wraps it in linen, verse 46. The dead Jesus is real, confirmed by the centurion, verse 45. Paul's earliest creed puts the burial between death and resurrection, 1 Corinthians 15:3-4, to show that He truly died and that the rising was no mere recovery.
study.god:
The chapter shows a God who is sovereign over the worst thing that human beings ever did. Every human actor in it has his reasons: envy in the priests, fear in Pilate, appetite for spectacle in the soldiers. Yet Peter says on the day of Pentecost that Jesus was 'handed over by God's set purpose and foreknowledge,' Acts 2:23, and Isaiah says it was 'the LORD's will to crush Him,' Isaiah 53:10. Mark holds both truths without explaining them. The people are really guilty, and God is really in command, and the passion is not an accident that slipped past Him.

God is just and holy. The darkness from noon to three is the hand of God in judgment, as Amos 8:9 had said it would be, and it falls on the day when His Son bears sin. This is the same God who 'did not spare His own Son,' Romans 8:32. His holiness is not softened for the sake of His love; His love goes through His holiness to the cross. To read the cry of verse 34 as anything other than serious is to flatten what Mark has written.

God is silent in this chapter, and the silence is part of the revelation. There is no voice from heaven, as at the baptism and the transfiguration, Mark 1:11 and 9:7. The Father does not intervene to answer the taunt, 'let Him come down.' Yet the silence is not absence. At the moment of death God acts, and what He does is tear the veil, verse 38. The one who does not speak to the mockers speaks through the sign.

God is the one who opens the way. The veil in Exodus 26 was His own design, to keep sinners from the holiest place while still dwelling among them. Now He rends His own barrier. That means the distance between God and sinners was never ultimately a matter of walls, and the removal of the wall is as much God's own initiative as its construction.

God is the God of the nations. Psalm 22 ends with 'all the families of the nations' bowing before the LORD, Psalm 22:27, and the first voice raised at the cross is a Roman soldier's. The God of Israel was always going to be the God of the whole earth.

For worship this chapter asks for silence before it asks for song. A person who has stood at this cross does not boast of their own goodness, as Pilate's hands, the priests' piety and Peter's earlier promise all fail. They look at the Son forsaken in their place, and they hear the Father's answer in what happens next, which Mark will let the women discover at dawn.

crossReferences.note: The cry from the cross is the psalm's first line. David writes of being 'so far from saving me' while still calling God 'my God.' Jesus takes the words of every abandoned believer and brings them to the cross, where the abandonment is real and the trust does not let go.

'They divide my garments among them and cast lots for my clothing.' Mark 15:24 reports exactly this. Soldiers at the foot of the cross, indifferent to what they are doing, fulfill a line David wrote a thousand years earlier, showing that even the casual cruelty of the execution was within God's plan.

The servant 'did not open His mouth,' like a lamb before its shearers. Jesus' silence before Pilate, Mark 15:5, is not weakness or evasion but the fulfilment of this picture. He answers the one question that matters and refuses to defend Himself against the rest.

God says that in the day of judgment He will 'make the sun go down at noon.' The three hours of darkness in Mark 15:33 take place at midday, and the connection hints that the cross is the day of the LORD in miniature, when judgment falls on One in place of many.

At the baptism the heavens are torn and the Father calls Jesus 'My beloved Son.' At the cross the veil is torn and a centurion calls Him Son of God. The same verb frames the Gospel's story, showing that the sonship declared at the Jordan is the sonship proved at Golgotha.

'The Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many.' This verse is the key to the cross. It explains why Jesus will not come down: the ransom is paid by staying, and what looks like helpless defeat is the purpose He announced.

God's instructions for the curtain that 'will separate the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place.' Cherubim were woven into it, as at Eden's gate in Genesis 3:24. It was the visible sign that sinners could not simply walk into God's presence. The tearing of Mark 15:38 removes what this verse built.

The preacher to the Hebrews says believers have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place 'by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body.' The tearing of the veil is read as Christ's own body opening the way to God.

Paul says Christ 'redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us,' quoting Deuteronomy 21:23, 'Cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree.' This explains the shame of crucifixion in Mark 15 as the very place where the curse due to others is taken.

God 'made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf.' The sentence is the theology of Barabbas going free. Jesus, who is innocent as Pilate admits, verse 14, is treated as the guilty one so that guilty people may be treated as righteous in Him.

'He who did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all.' The verb for 'gave up' is the Gospel's paradidomi. What Judas, the priests and Pilate did in malice, the Father did in love, and the same event is both crime and gift.

A body hung on a tree must be buried before nightfall, because the hanged man is 'under God's curse' and must not defile the land. This explains the urgency of Joseph of Arimathea in Mark 15:42-46 and shows why a tomb, not a pit, was a mercy.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story begins with a man and woman who reached for what was not theirs and were sent from God's presence, and it has been asking ever since how the way back could be opened. Genesis 3 ended with cherubim and a flaming sword at the gate. The tabernacle repeated the picture with a curtain of cherubim, Exodus 26:31. The prophets spoke of a servant who would carry what the people could not, Isaiah 53:4-6, and a righteous sufferer whose suffering would end in the praise of the nations, Psalm 22:27. Mark 15 is where those lines meet in one afternoon.

At Golgotha the first Adam's failure is answered by the last Adam's obedience. Where Adam grasped, Jesus is stripped; where Adam hid among the trees, Jesus is lifted on one, Galatians 3:13. The curse of Genesis 3:17, thorns from the ground, is on His head. The promise of a seed who would be struck in the heel while crushing the serpent's head, Genesis 3:15, is fulfilled in the wound that breaks death's hold, Hebrews 2:14. The flaming sword is not lifted by a bargain but by a death, and the veil is torn from the top, so that God opens His own house.

Israel's story is gathered up here as well. The people who had been taken out of Egypt by the blood of a lamb now see the Lamb of God slain at Passover. The temple that stood as the meeting place of heaven and earth is judged and replaced by the body of the One whose death opens God to the nations. A centurion, from the people Israel had been called to bless, confesses what Israel's own rulers had denied.

This is not yet the end. The tomb is sealed and the women are watching, which is where the chapter stops. The empty tomb is still to come, and beyond it the commission to every creature, and beyond that the day when 'He will wipe away every tear,' Revelation 21:4, and the throne of God and of the Lamb stands where the curse once was, Revelation 22:1-3. The King who reigned from a cross will reign over a renewed creation, and the way that was shut at Eden stands open for ever.

quiz.q: What does the release of Barabbas in place of Jesus illustrate?

options.text: Substitution: the guilty man goes free while the innocent Son dies in his place.
options.note: Barabbas the murderer is released while Jesus is condemned, a living picture of substitution.

options.text: That Pilate was a fair and impartial judge.
options.note: Pilate acted to please the crowd against his own sense of Jesus' innocence; the point is substitution.

options.text: That the crowd made a tragic mistake in their choice.
options.note: The crowd did choose wrongly, but the deeper meaning is the innocent dying for the guilty.

options.text: The innocent taking the place of the guilty, as at the heart of the gospel.
options.note: Correct in substance, but it should name Barabbas specifically as the guilty man set free.

quiz.q: What is ironic about the mockery, He saved others, but He cannot save Himself?

options.text: He saves others precisely by refusing to save Himself, staying on the cross to bear their judgment.
options.note: The mockers speak truer than they know; His not coming down is how He saves, Mark 15:31.

options.text: He was actually unable to come down from the cross.
options.note: He could have come down; He chose to remain in order to save others.

options.text: The mockers accidentally spoke a deep truth about His saving death.
options.note: True, but it should state that His refusal to save Himself is the very means of saving others.

options.text: The mockery had no significance at all.
options.note: Mark records the irony deliberately: their taunt unwittingly states the gospel.

quiz.q: What did Jesus' cry, My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me, express?

options.text: His real bearing of God's judgment and forsakenness in the place of sinners, in the words of Psalm 22.
options.note: Mark 15:34; genuine forsakenness for sin, voiced through the psalm that ends in vindication.

options.text: That Jesus had lost His faith in God.
options.note: It is a prayer to God, quoting Scripture; anguish held within trust, not lost faith.

options.text: The depth of His suffering as He bore judgment for sin.
options.note: Correct in substance, but it should note He voices the real forsakenness in the words of Psalm 22.

options.text: A simple expression of physical pain.
options.note: The cry expresses a far deeper anguish than physical pain: God-forsakenness for sin.

quiz.q: What did the tearing of the temple veil at Jesus' death signify?

options.text: That the way to God is now opened through Christ's death, and the old temple order is ending.
options.note: Torn from top to bottom by God, the veil signals open access to God, Hebrews 10:19-20.

options.text: That the temple building had simply grown old and worn.
options.note: The tearing was a divine sign at the moment of Jesus' death, not natural wear.

options.text: That access to God's presence is now open through the cross.
options.note: True, but it should also include the judgment on the old temple order that the tearing signals.

options.text: That worship in the temple should now be more careful.
options.note: The torn veil points to open access through Christ, not to more careful temple ritual.

quiz.q: Who confessed the truth about Jesus at His death, and what did he say?

options.text: A Gentile centurion said, Truly this man was the Son of God, the confession Mark's Gospel aimed toward.
options.note: Mark 15:39 forms an inclusio with Mark 1:1, now confessed by a Gentile soldier.

options.text: The chief priests admitted He was the Messiah.
options.note: The priests mocked Him; it was the centurion who confessed Him the Son of God.

options.text: A Roman soldier acknowledged Jesus as the Son of God.
options.note: Correct, but it should note how this confession fulfils Mark's opening line about the Son of God.

options.text: The two robbers proclaimed Him King of Israel.
options.note: The robbers berated Him; the centurion made the great confession.

questions: Barabbas the guilty went free because Jesus the innocent took his place. How does it move you to see yourself in Barabbas, released because Christ died in your place?
Jesus was mocked as King even as He truly reigned from the cross. Where do you need eyes to see God's power and kingship in what looks like weakness or defeat?
Jesus saved others by not saving Himself. How does His refusal to come down from the cross reshape your understanding of love and sacrifice?
At the cross the way to God was torn open. How does the truth that you now have direct access to God through Christ change the way you approach Him?
A hardened Gentile soldier looked at the crucified Jesus and confessed Him the Son of God. As you look at the cross, what confession does it draw from you?

translationNotes.note: The BSB does not print a verse 28; the words some manuscripts add, He was numbered with the transgressors from Isaiah 53:12, are absent from the earliest witnesses here, so the numbering skips from 27 to 29, though the truth they state is fulfilled in the scene.
Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani is Aramaic, quoting Psalm 22:1; Mark preserves Jesus' actual words and translates them, My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me.
The veil torn from top to bottom indicates a divine act from heaven's side; it opens the way into God's presence, as Hebrews 10:19-20 explains, and marks the end of the old temple order.
